lead: The principle of inclusion and exclusion (PIE) corrects overcounting when sets overlap. Adding the sizes of sets counts shared elements more than once. PIE subtracts pairwise intersections, adds back triple intersections, and alternates signs for more sets. It converts a question about at least one property into counts of intersections. Use it for divisibility counts, forbidden positions, and onto functions. Plain addition fails when categories overlap, as with numbers divisible by 2 or 3.
prereq: You need: 3.1 sum and product rules for adding disjoint cases, and Unit 2 for set union, intersection and complement.

blocks.text: Let A and B be finite sets. The symbol |A| means the number of elements in A. The union A∪B is the set of elements in A, in B, or in both. The intersection A∩B is the set of elements in both.

blocks.where: A and B are finite sets; |A| is the size of A; ∩ is intersection; ∪ is union.

blocks.text: Proof by regions. Split A∪B into three disjoint parts: elements only in A, elements only in B, elements in both. The sum |A|+|B| counts the middle part twice. Subtract |A∩B| once, and every element is counted once. If A and B are disjoint, A∩B is empty and |A∩B|=0, so the formula reduces to the sum rule in 3.1.

The idea is correction. Add everything, then remove the excess. For two overlapping lists, say students who passed maths and students who passed physics, the overlap is counted in both lists, so subtract it once.

sections.h3: Three sets: subtract pairs, add the triple

blocks.where: A, B and C are finite sets; |A∩B| is the number of elements in both A and B; |A∩B∩C| is the number in all three.

blocks.text: An element in exactly one set is counted once by the three single terms and never subtracted. An element in exactly two sets is counted twice by the singles, then subtracted once by its pair term, leaving 1. An element in all three sets is counted 3 times by the singles, subtracted 3 times by the three pair terms, giving 0, so |A∩B∩C| adds it back once. Every element of the union is counted exactly once.
Some syllabi write PIE for this principle. The signs alternate: plus for one set, minus for two, plus for three. For k sets, add k-fold intersections with sign (−1)<sup>k+1</sup>.
Many questions ask for none or not. Let U be the universal set. The complement of A∪B∪C is U−(A∪B∪C). Its size is |U|−|A∪B∪C|. Count the union first, then subtract from |U|.
number of multiples of d in 1..n = ⌊n/d⌋
blocks.where: d is a positive integer; n is the upper limit; ⌊x⌋ is the greatest integer ≤ x.

blocks.text: The reason is that the multiples are d, 2d, …, kd, and kd ≤ n < (k+1)d, so k = ⌊n/d⌋. For an intersection of multiples, use the least common multiple, not the product. The multiples of both d and e are the multiples of lcm(d,e). So |A∩B| = ⌊n/lcm(d,e)⌋. For 2 and 3, lcm is 6. For 4 and 6, lcm is 12, not 24. For 2, 3 and 5, lcm is 30.
For a general range a to b, count in 1 to b and subtract count in 1 to a−1. If the range does not end at a multiple of d, ⌊b/d⌋ still works; n/2 without floor is wrong.
Divisibility counts are the standard use. The worked example below counts integers divisible by 2, 3 or 5. The same method counts integers divisible by none, by complement.

Forbidden positions. Suppose n items must be placed in n positions, but some item-position pairs are forbidden. Let Ai be the set of arrangements in which item i sits in one of its forbidden positions; the derangement case is when each item has exactly one forbidden position. Count arrangements that avoid every Ai by PIE over the forbidden events; see 3.8.

blocks.where: m is the domain size; n is the codomain size; C(n,k) is the number of ways to choose k of n elements; onto(m,n) is the number of onto functions from an m-set to an n-set.

blocks.text: In the onto formula, C(n,k) chooses k missed codomain elements, and (n−k)<sup>m</sup> counts functions into the remaining elements. The k=0 term is n<sup>m</sup>. The alternating signs remove functions missing at least one element. If n>m the answer is 0.

figure.caption: For numbers from 1 to 100, the Even circle shows 50, the Multiple of 3 circle shows 33, and the Multiple of 5 circle shows 20. Only these three circle totals are shown; the overlap regions are not drawn. The plain sum 50+33+20 overcounts shared multiples, so intersections must be subtracted.

spec.aria: Three overlapping circles are labelled Even, Multiple of 3 and Multiple of 5. For numbers up to 100, the circle totals are 50, 33 and 20; overlap regions are not drawn.

examples.question: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2, 3 or 5?
steps: Let U = {1, 2, …, 100}. Let A be the integers in U divisible by 2, B those divisible by 3, and C those divisible by 5.
Count pairwise intersections using least common multiples. |A∩B| = ⌊100/lcm(2,3)⌋ = ⌊100/6⌋ = 16. |A∩C| = ⌊100/lcm(2,5)⌋ = ⌊100/10⌋ = 10. |B∩C| = ⌊100/lcm(3,5)⌋ = ⌊100/15⌋ = 6.
examples.answer: 74 integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2, 3 or 5.
examples.check:
n = 100
A = n // 2
B = n // 3
C = n // 5
AB = n // 6
AC = n // 10
BC = n // 15
ABC = n // 30
total = A + B + C - AB - AC - BC + ABC
print(total)

traps: Forgetting to add the triple intersection |A∩B∩C| back after subtracting the three pairwise intersections.
Using n/2 without floor when the range does not end at a multiple of d. Use ⌊n/d⌋.
Using the product d·e instead of lcm(d,e) for the intersection of multiples of d and e. For 4 and 6, use 12, not 24.
Confusing at least one with none. For none, subtract the union from the universal set: |U| − |A∪B∪C|.
In the onto-function formula, a sign error or starting the sum at k=1 instead of k=0. The k=0 term is n^m.

quiz.q: State the two-set inclusion-exclusion formula for |A∪B|.
Why is |A∩B| subtracted only once in |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B|?
quiz.a: The sum |A|+|B| counts each element of A∩B twice, once in A and once in B. To count it once, subtract one copy, so subtract |A∩B| once.

quiz.q: How many integers from 1 to 60 are divisible by 4 or 6?
From 1 to 100, how many integers are divisible by none of 2, 3 or 5?
quiz.a: By the worked example, the union has 74 integers. The complement has 100 − 74 = 26.

quiz.q: A student writes |A∪B∪C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A∩B| − |A∩C| − |B∩C|. Which elements are counted wrongly?
quiz.a: Elements in all three sets are counted 3 times by the single terms and subtracted 3 times by the pair terms, giving 0. They must be added back once by +|A∩B∩C|. Other regions are correct.

quiz.q: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2 or 3 but not by 5?
quiz.a: Divisible by 2 or 3: 50 + 33 − 16 = 67. Among these, divisible by 5: multiples of 10 or 15, minus multiples of 30, giving 10 + 6 − 3 = 13. Answer: 67 − 13 = 54.

quiz.q: Write the complement-counting formula for the number of elements in U that lie in none of A, B, C.
How many onto functions are there from a 5-element set to a 3-element set?

beyond: Not for the exam. PIE is the first of the sieve methods; the general sieve formula and Bonferroni inequalities bound unions when only some intersections are known. Rook polynomials organise forbidden-position counts for boards, and network reliability uses inclusion-exclusion over failed links. Search terms: inclusion-exclusion sieve, rook polynomial, Bonferroni inequalities.
